newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Brittan says WTO deadlines crucial for credibility.
newsitem.headline: Brittan says WTO deadlines crucial for credibility.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) must meet deadlines set after the Uruguay Round of talks to maintain credibility and further liberalise world trade, European Commission vice-president Sir Leon Brittan said on Tuesday.

"The WTO will only advance if we make a success of the talks that are now under way," Brittan told delegates to the 1996 Europe/East Asia Economic Summit in Hong Kong organised by the World Economic Forum.
"If we fail on these short-term objectives, the world will look askance and with scepticism at our long-term strategy, which will be blown off course. Let us not allow that to happen."
Two deadlines hang over the WTO ministerial conference in Singapore on December 9-13. They concern agreements on the liberalisation of the telecommunications and financial services industries.

"If we fail on either of these, the WTO will lack the credibility needed to lay sound foundations for the next round of trade liberalisation that I believe is needed and that will start by the end of the century," Brittan said.

Agreements to liberalise trade in telecommunications, financial services, maritime and professional services all fall under unfinished business left from the Uruguay Round of trade talks at the end of 1993, said Jesus Seade, deputy director general of the WTO.

The Uruguay Round of talks, established in 1986 under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), created a mechanism for lowering trade barriers by the year 2000. It ended in 1994 while the WTO was being established to replace GATT.

While members have until 1997 to reach agreement on the liberalisation of financial services, some urgency has arisen in talks on the telecommunications industry after the tabling last week of new proposals from the European Union and the United States, he said.
"On telecoms, the time is ripe for a better definition of positions because it has to be completed in the initial months of the year," Seade said.
"And the two offers from the U.S. and the Europeans are very, very interesting, very attractive, and the general atmosphere in the negotiations right now is quite upbeat."
Brittan challenged Asian nations to respond to the telecommunications initiative from the United States and European Union to ensure that the WTO achieves agreement on a crucial industry.

"Those in Asia who care about the WTO, and I know there are many, must ensure that Asian partners now match that lead," Brittan said. "The WTO needs a specific, concrete success and success means bigger market access offers from everybody now."

He acknowledged that more assistance was needed for developing nations confronting these demands. Neither increased technical assistance or increased market access would solve the problems of the least-developed countries, he said.

"(Europe) looks to our developed-country partners as well as the rich and developing countries to bind themselves with us at Singapore to do something new for the least-developed countries rather than simply to claim that they are doing a great deal already," Brittan said.
